notes.19: Interface atomic fraction depends on ratio of grain size and thickness; small grains explain as-quenched thickness below sample A.
notes.23: Light B and heavy Zr do not contribute to measured partial Fe-projected DOS.

source_interpretation.text: The authors use annealing to vary the relative amount of nanograins and intercrystalline material, then combine CEMS fractions with iron-projected phonon spectra. They seek to determine whether anomalous low/high-energy vibrations belong to grain interiors or interfaces; the separated spectra depend on a two-component model rather than isolated-grain measurements.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Motivation, CEMS and Equation 1

source_interpretation.topic: Thermal history changes more than grain diameter
source_interpretation.text: For samples A–D, the fitted interface atomic fraction drops from 0.51 to 0.11 while mean grain size grows from 10.9 to 14.9 nm. The authors interpret this as an increase mainly in grain number/fraction. The as-quenched material already contains 2.2 nm grains. DSC transitions 783(1) K and 1017(1) K are characterization results, not missing synthesis setpoints.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Table I, preparation and annealing discussion

source_interpretation.text: Equation 1 writes g(E)=(1−XIC)gNG(E)+XICgIC(E). Reference grain/interface spectra are derived using A and C, initially assuming only weak variation with grain size. Figures 3–4 compare the as-quenched, B and D component spectra with those references. This assumption and subsequent tests must remain visible when reusing the spectra.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Equation 1 and Figures2b,3,4

source_interpretation.topic: Thin interfaces can acquire grain-like vibrations
source_interpretation.text: The derived interface spectrum for D, whose mean model thickness is 0.6(5) nm, develops peaks near 23, 27 and 36 meV and loses low-energy states below 20 meV. The authors suggest that an interface about two atomic layers or thinner can acquire neighboring-grain vibrational properties. This is an interpretation of the component model, not an atom-resolved interface image.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure4c and thickness interpretation

source_interpretation.topic: Interface fraction, low-energy modes and design implications
source_interpretation.text: The fitted low-energy DOS remains quadratic over 2–12 meV. The normalized coefficient varies approximately linearly with interface fraction; extrapolated endpoints are 1 for bulk Fe and 2.9 for the reference interface spectrum. The authors therefore propose controlling grain fraction to tune thermoelastic behavior. Entropy, displacement, force-constant and specific-heat trends are mentioned without numerical sample results and are not exported as extra measured properties.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figure 5, low-energy analysis and conclusion

source_interpretation.topic: Measurement basis and missing chemical detail
source_interpretation.text: The measured DOS is Fe-projected: B and Zr contributions are excluded by definition (note 23). The source reports 63% enrichment of iron in 57Fe, but no raw-alloy synthesis or detailed melt-spinning settings. Reported grain lattice constants refer to α-Fe, not to a crystalline Fe90Zr7B3 unit cell. No specimen atom coordinates, TEM image or grain-shape distribution is supplied in this main.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 1,4, Preparation, structural methods and note 23

source_interpretation.topic: Thickness trend is not globally monotonic
source_interpretation.text: Table I gives 1.0(5) nm for the as-quenched interface and 2.3(5) nm for A; note 19 explains that the derived thickness depends on grain size as well as interface fraction. The subsequent A–D decrease must not be misrepresented as a monotonic decrease from the as-quenched state.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 1,4, Table I and note19
